title: Biggest Tank Between Two Walls
statement:
You get an array heights. Position i holds a thin vertical wall of height heights[i], and neighbouring walls are 1 unit apart.

Pick two walls i < j. Together with the floor they form a tank. The water level cannot rise above the shorter of the two walls, and the walls in between do not matter. The tank holds min(heights[i], heights[j]) × (j − i) units.

Return the largest amount any pair of walls can hold.

examples.why: Walls 0 and 6: min(5, 9) × 6 = 30. The two tallest walls are neighbours and hold only 9.
Walls 1 and 3: min(9, 8) × 2 = 16. The widest pair, the two outer walls, holds only 1 × 4 = 4.

hints: Start with the widest tank, the two outer walls. To find a bigger one you must give up width. Which wall is worth giving up?
Suppose the left wall is the shorter one. Every other tank that uses it is narrower and still capped by its height. Can any of them beat the current tank?
Keep a pointer at each end, record the area, and always move the pointer at the shorter wall inward.

explain.intuition:
Start with the two outer walls, the widest tank. Say the left wall is shorter. Any other tank that uses this left wall is narrower, and its level is still at most the left wall's height. So none of them can beat the tank you just measured. The left wall is done: drop it and move inward. If the right wall is shorter, drop it instead.

Each step throws away one wall that provably cannot be part of a better answer, so n − 1 steps check everything that matters. Moving the taller wall is the classic mistake: the level stays capped by the same short wall while the width shrinks, so you can only lose.
steps: While lo < hi: compute min(heights[lo], heights[hi]) × (hi − lo) and update best.
Move the pointer at the shorter wall inward. On a tie, moving either one is safe.
pitfalls: Moving the pointer at the taller wall. The shorter wall still caps the level and the width drops, so you skip the tanks that could have been better.
Assuming the two tallest walls win. In [5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 9, 9] they are neighbours and hold 9; the answer is 30.
Counting the walls in between as obstacles or as volume. Only the two chosen walls matter.

solutions.title: Every pair
solutions.idea: Measure every pair of walls and keep the best. Correct, but quadratic.

solutions.title: Two pointers, drop the shorter wall
solutions.idea: Start wide. The shorter wall cannot do better with any closer partner, so measure it once and move past it.

followups: Return the pair of positions instead of the amount. Which pair do you return on a tie?
Now the walls in between do block the water, and every dip fills up. How much water is held in total? (That is a different problem.)
